chapter_text:
CHAPTER 1 — SETS

Introduction

The idea of a 'set' is one of the simplest in mathematics and at the same time one of the most powerful. Almost every modern mathematical structure — from numbers to functions to algebraic systems — is built on top of sets. In this chapter we learn what a set is, how to write one down, the different kinds of sets, how to compare and combine them, and the laws (especially De Morgan's laws) that govern set operations.

1.1 SETS AND THEIR REPRESENTATION

A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. 'Well-defined' means we can decide unambiguously whether a given object belongs to the collection or not. The objects in a set are called its elements (or members). Sets are denoted by capital letters (A, B, C, ...) and their elements by lower-case letters (a, b, c, ...). We write a ∈ A to mean 'a is an element of A' and a ∉ A to mean 'a is not an element of A'.

A set can be specified in two ways. The ROSTER (or tabular) method lists every element separated by commas, enclosed in curly braces: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The SET-BUILDER form gives a property that characterises every element: A = {x : x ∈ N and x < 6}, read as 'A is the set of all x such that x is a natural number and x is less than 6'.

1.2 TYPES OF SETS

The EMPTY (or null) set has no elements; it is written ∅ or { }. A SINGLETON set has exactly one element. A FINITE set has a definite, countable number of elements; an INFINITE set does not. Two sets are EQUAL when they have exactly the same elements (order and repetition do not matter): {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2}. Two sets are EQUIVALENT when they have the same NUMBER of elements (cardinality), even if the elements differ. Sets are DISJOINT when they have no element in common.

1.3 SUBSETS AND POWER SETS

A is a SUBSET of B (written A ⊆ B) when every element of A is also an element of B. Every set is a subset of itself: A ⊆ A. The empty set is a subset of every set: ∅ ⊆ A. If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A then A = B. A is a PROPER subset of B (A ⊂ B) when A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.

The POWER SET of A, written P(A), is the set whose elements are all the subsets of A. If A has n elements, P(A) has 2^n elements.

1.4 UNIVERSAL SET AND VENN DIAGRAMS

In any particular discussion we usually fix a UNIVERSAL set U that contains every object under consideration. All other sets in the discussion are subsets of U.

VENN diagrams are a pictorial way to represent sets: U is drawn as a rectangle and other sets as circles inside it. Operations on sets are visualised by which regions of the diagram are shaded.

1.5 OPERATIONS ON SETS

The UNION A ∪ B is the set of all elements that belong to A or to B (or both): A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
The INTERSECTION A ∩ B is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
The DIFFERENCE A − B (or A \ B) is the set of all elements that are in A but not in B: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}. Note A − B ≠ B − A in general.
The COMPLEMENT of A (with respect to the universal set U), written A' or A^c, is U − A.

Key identities: A ∪ A' = U, A ∩ A' = ∅, (A')' = A, U' = ∅.

1.6 DE MORGAN'S LAWS

De Morgan's laws link union, intersection and complement:
  (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'
  (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'

They say that the complement of a union is the intersection of complements, and vice versa. These two identities are workhorses for simplifying set expressions and proving identities.

SUMMARY

- A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects; specified by roster or by set-builder notation.
- Types: empty (∅), singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent, disjoint, subset (⊆), proper subset (⊂).
- Power set P(A) has 2^n elements if |A| = n.
- Universal set U; Venn diagrams give a picture of set operations.
- Operations: union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (−), complement (').
- De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

learning_outcomes.description: Define a set and express a given set in both roster and set-builder forms.
Identify a set as empty, singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent or disjoint.
List all subsets of a given finite set and compute the number of subsets using |P(A)| = 2^n.
Distinguish a subset from a proper subset and use ⊆, ⊂, =.
Draw Venn diagrams to represent given sets and their relationships within a universal set.
Compute A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A − B and A' for given finite sets.
Verify or refute proposed set identities by substituting concrete sets.
State and verify De Morgan's laws with concrete sets; use them to simplify set expressions.

chapter_summary.title: Sets — NIOS Official Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics (311) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 1: Sets. It covers the idea of a set, its representations (roster and set-builder), the main types of sets, subsets and the power set, universal sets and Venn diagrams, operations on sets (union, intersection, difference, complement) and De Morgan's laws.

sections.heading: Sets and Their Representation
bullets: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects.
Sets are denoted by capital letters; elements by small letters.
Roster (tabular) form lists all elements: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
Set-builder form gives a property: A = {x : x ∈ N and x < 6}.

sections.heading: Classification of Sets
bullets: Empty / null set: no elements (∅ or { }).
Singleton set: exactly one element.
Finite vs infinite sets: definite count vs not.
Equal sets: same elements regardless of order. Equivalent sets: same number of elements.
Disjoint sets: no element in common.

sections.heading: Subsets and Power Sets
bullets: A ⊆ B iff every element of A is in B.
Every set is a subset of itself; ∅ is a subset of every set.
If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A then A = B.
If A ⊆ B and A ≠ B then A is a proper subset, A ⊂ B.
If |A| = n, then |P(A)| = 2^n (P(A) is the power set, the set of all subsets of A).

sections.heading: Universal Set and Venn Diagrams
bullets: The universal set U is the set of all objects pertaining to a particular problem.
Venn diagrams represent the universal set by the interior of a rectangle and other sets by circles inside it.
Set operations correspond to shaded regions in the Venn diagram.

sections.heading: Complement of a Set
bullets: A' = U − A: the elements of U that are not in A.
A ∪ A' = U.

sections.heading: Operations on Sets
bullets: Union: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
Intersection: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
Difference: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}. Generally A − B ≠ B − A.
Complement: A' = U − A (defined with respect to a universal set U).

sections.heading: De Morgan's Laws
bullets: These two identities turn unions into intersections (and vice versa) under complementation.

key_takeaways: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects; it has two standard representations — roster and set-builder.
Subsets and the power set: |P(A)| = 2^n for |A| = n.
Union, intersection, difference and complement are the four basic operations on sets.
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
Venn diagrams give a picture-based way to verify any of these identities.

glossary.definition: A well-defined collection of distinct objects.
A way of writing a set by listing all its elements separated by commas, enclosed in curly braces, e.g. {1, 2, 3}.
A way of writing a set by giving a property that all its elements satisfy, e.g. {x : x ∈ N and x < 6}.
The set with no elements, denoted ∅ or { }.
A set with exactly one element.
Sets with exactly the same elements.
Sets with the same number of elements (cardinality), even if the elements differ.
A is a subset of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is an element of B.
A is a proper subset of B (A ⊂ B) if A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.
The set of all subsets of a given set A, denoted P(A). |P(A)| = 2^|A|.
The set of all objects pertaining to a particular problem; denoted U. Every other set in the discussion is a subset of U.
The complement A' of A is the set of all elements of the universal set U that are not in A: A' = U − A.
A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — all elements in A, B, or both.
A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — elements common to both.
(A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B' — the duality between union and intersection under complementation.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Sets (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics (311) official Worksheet-1 for Lesson 1: Sets. Attempt all questions. Show your reasoning and intermediate sets clearly.

questions.question: Write three different sets in the roster method by taking different objects in your surroundings.
questions.answer: Example answers: (1) Set of three primary colours: {red, yellow, blue}. (2) Set of vowels in the word 'mathematics': {a, e, i}. (3) Set of even numbers in the first 10 natural numbers: {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}. Any three distinct sets with their elements listed inside curly braces are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Look for three sets with elements explicitly listed, comma-separated, inside braces.

questions.question: Develop any three sets in the set-builder form by using any type of numbers in the number system.
questions.answer: Example answers: (1) {x : x ∈ N and x is odd, x < 10} = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}. (2) {x : x ∈ Z and −3 ≤ x ≤ 3} = {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. (3) {x : x ∈ Q and 0 < x < 1, denominator 2} = {1/2}. Any three sets stated in set-builder form with a clear property are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Set-builder form: {x : P(x)} where P is the defining property. Include the universe (N, Z, Q, R) and the constraint.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and B = {5, 6, 7}, find (i) A − B and (ii) B − A. Are they equal?
questions.answer: (i) A − B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 8} (elements in A but not in B). (ii) B − A = ∅ (every element of B is also in A). A − B ≠ B − A in general. Here A − B has 5 elements while B − A has 0, so they are clearly not equal.
questions.explanation: Set difference is not commutative: A − B picks elements of A absent from B; B − A picks elements of B absent from A.

questions.question: If A = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, B = {5, 6, 7, 8} and C = {7, 8, 9}, find (i) A ∩ (B ∩ C) and (ii) A ∪ (B ∪ C).
questions.explanation: Apply intersection / union one step at a time; ∪ and ∩ are both associative and commutative.

questions.question: Given A = {x : x ∈ Z and x < 6} and B = {y : y is a prime number, y < 10}, find (i) A ∪ B and (ii) A ∩ B.
questions.answer: A = {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (all integers strictly less than 6). B = {2, 3, 5, 7}. (i) A ∪ B = {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7}. (ii) A ∩ B = {2, 3, 5} (the primes less than 6 that are in A).
questions.explanation: Note that 7 ∈ B but 7 ∉ A (since 7 ≥ 6); and 2, 3, 5 are in both A and B.

questions.question: Write down all the subsets of (i) A = {a, b} and (ii) B = {1, 2, 3}. Observe the relationship between the number of elements and the number of subsets.
questions.answer:
(i) Subsets of A: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}. That is 4 = 2² subsets.
(ii) Subsets of B: ∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3}. That is 8 = 2³ subsets.

Observation: a set with n elements has exactly 2^n subsets — including the empty set and the set itself. This is the size of the power set: |P(A)| = 2^|A|.
questions.explanation: Each element can either belong to a subset or not — giving 2 choices per element. n elements ⇒ 2^n possible subsets.

questions.question: Give an example of sets A and B where A is a subset of B. Draw Venn diagrams for A − B and B − A when A ⊆ B.
questions.answer:
Example: A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Then A ⊆ B.

A − B = ∅ (every element of A is also in B, so there's nothing to remove).
B − A = {3, 4} (the elements of B that are not in A).

Venn diagram: draw two circles, one (B) larger and one (A) entirely INSIDE B. The region of A unshaded is A − B = ∅. The region of B outside A is B − A. The picture shows that when A ⊆ B, the difference A − B vanishes while B − A is the 'shell' of B outside A.
questions.explanation: When A ⊆ B, A is entirely inside B in the Venn diagram. So A − B = ∅ and B − A is the part of B outside A.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, A = {1, 3, 5, 7} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, verify (i) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
questions.explanation: Compute each side independently and compare. Here A and B happen to be a partition of U, so the verification is particularly clean.

questions.question: Let N be the universal set of natural numbers and let A and B be its subsets given by A = {x : x ∈ N and x < 10} and B = {x : x ∈ N and x is a multiple of 5}. Find the complements of A and B.
questions.answer:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} (natural numbers less than 10).
B = {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, ...} (multiples of 5 in N).

A' = N − A = {x : x ∈ N and x ≥ 10} = {10, 11, 12, 13, ...} — every natural number from 10 onwards.

B' = N − B = {x : x ∈ N and x is NOT a multiple of 5} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, ...} — every natural number that does not end in 0 or 5.

Note: complements are taken with respect to the universal set N. Both complements are infinite sets.
questions.explanation: Take A' = U − A directly. For the multiples-of-5 case, list a few elements to make the pattern clear.

questions.question: Let U = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16}, A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, B = {10, 12, 14, 16}. Verify (i) (A')' = A, (ii) A ∪ A' = U, (iii) (B')' = B.
questions.answer:
A' = U − A = {10, 12, 14, 16} = B (coincidentally).
B' = U − B = {2, 4, 6, 8} = A.

(i) (A')' = (B)' = A. Indeed (A')' = A ✓.
(ii) A ∪ A' = {2, 4, 6, 8} ∪ {10, 12, 14, 16} = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16} = U ✓.
(iii) (B')' = (A)' = B. Indeed (B')' = B ✓.

General conclusion: the complement is an INVOLUTION — applying it twice returns the original set. And every element of U lies in exactly one of A or A', confirming A ∪ A' = U and A ∩ A' = ∅.
questions.explanation: Compute A', B', then take complements again and verify equality with the original sets.

questions.explanation: Order does not matter in a set; both are the same set.

questions.question: The empty set has no elements at all.
questions.explanation: By definition |∅| = 0.

questions.question: Two equal sets are always equivalent.
questions.explanation: Equal sets have identical elements, so they trivially have the same cardinality (i.e. are equivalent).

questions.question: Two equivalent sets are always equal.
questions.explanation: Equivalent only means same cardinality. {1,2,3} and {a,b,c} are equivalent but not equal.

questions.question: If |A| = n, then A has exactly 2^n subsets.
Every set is a subset of itself.
questions.explanation: A ⊆ A holds vacuously by the definition of subset.

questions.question: The empty set is a subset of every set.
questions.explanation: There is no element of ∅ that fails to be in A, so ∅ ⊆ A for all A.

questions.question: Every set is a PROPER subset of itself.
questions.explanation: A proper subset is strictly smaller. A is not a proper subset of itself.

questions.question: Set intersection is commutative: A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
questions.explanation: 'x ∈ A and x ∈ B' is logically the same as 'x ∈ B and x ∈ A'.

questions.question: Set difference is commutative: A − B = B − A.
questions.explanation: Usually A − B ≠ B − A. Example: A={1,2}, B={2,3}: A−B = {1}, B−A = {3}.

questions.question: For any sets A and B, A ∪ B ⊆ A whenever A ⊇ B.
questions.explanation: If A ⊇ B then B ⊆ A and A ∪ B = A, so A ∪ B ⊆ A.

questions.question: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
questions.explanation: It equals A' ∩ B' (De Morgan's first law).

questions.question: (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
questions.explanation: De Morgan's second law.

questions.question: If A ⊆ B, then A − B = ∅.
questions.explanation: Every element of A is also in B, so there's nothing in A that's not in B.

questions.question: For any sets A and B, n(A ∪ B) ≤ n(A) + n(B).
questions.explanation: By inclusion-exclusion n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B) ≤ n(A) + n(B).

questions.question: A ∩ A = A and A ∪ A = A for any set A.
questions.explanation: These are the idempotent laws of set operations.

questions.question: Set union is commutative: A ∪ B = B ∪ A.
questions.explanation: 'or' is commutative in logic, so the resulting sets are equal.

questions.question: Set union and intersection both distribute over each other: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
questions.explanation: This is the distributive law for sets; symmetric pair: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).

questions.question: Two sets with the same number of elements but different elements are called equal sets.
questions.explanation: That makes them EQUIVALENT, not equal. Equal sets must have the same elements.

questions.question: A set is a well-defined collection of ____ objects.
questions.explanation: Distinctness means no repetition; well-definedness ensures unambiguous membership.

questions.question: The notation x ∈ A means 'x ____ A'.
questions.answer: belongs to (or is an element of)
questions.explanation: ∈ is the membership symbol.

questions.question: The two main ways of representing a set are the ____ method and the set-builder form.
questions.explanation: Roster lists elements; set-builder gives a property.

questions.question: A set with no elements is called the ____ set.
questions.explanation: Denoted ∅ or { }.

questions.question: A set with exactly one element is called a ____ set.
questions.explanation: Example: {5}.

questions.question: If A has n elements, the number of subsets of A is ____.
questions.explanation: Each element either belongs to a subset or doesn't — 2 choices, n times.

questions.question: The set of all subsets of A is called the ____ of A and is denoted P(A).
The symbol ⊆ means 'is a ____ of'.
questions.explanation: A ⊆ B allows A = B; ⊂ is the proper-subset version.

questions.question: In a Venn diagram, the universal set U is represented by the interior of a ____.
questions.explanation: Standard convention; other sets are circles inside the rectangle.

questions.question: A ∪ B is the set of elements in A ____ B (or both).
questions.explanation: Union uses 'or' (inclusive).

questions.question: A ∩ B is the set of elements in A ____ B.
questions.explanation: Intersection uses 'and'.

questions.question: The complement of A with respect to U is given by A' = U ____ A.
questions.explanation: A' = U − A: elements of U not in A.

questions.question: A ∪ A' = ____.
questions.explanation: Every element of U is in A or in A'.

questions.question: By De Morgan's first law, (A ∪ B)' = ____.
questions.explanation: Complement of union is intersection of complements.

questions.question: By De Morgan's second law, (A ∩ B)' = ____.
questions.explanation: Complement of intersection is union of complements.

questions.question: What does it mean for a collection to be 'well-defined'? Give one example of a well-defined collection and one that is not.
questions.answer: A collection is well-defined if, given any candidate object, we can decide unambiguously whether it belongs to the collection or not. Well-defined example: 'the set of prime numbers less than 20' — we can check membership precisely. Not well-defined: 'the set of clever students in a school' — 'clever' has no precise membership rule, so different people will include different students.

questions.question: Write the set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ..., 20} in set-builder form.
questions.answer: {x : x is an even natural number and 2 ≤ x ≤ 20}, or equivalently {x : x = 2k, k ∈ N, 1 ≤ k ≤ 10}.

questions.question: Write {x : x ∈ N, 1 < x < 8} in roster form.
State the difference between equal and equivalent sets, with one example.
questions.answer: Two sets are EQUAL if they have exactly the same elements. Two sets are EQUIVALENT if they have the same number of elements (cardinality), regardless of what those elements are. Example: {1, 2, 3} and {3, 1, 2} are equal (same elements). {1, 2, 3} and {a, b, c} are equivalent (same size) but not equal. Equal ⇒ equivalent, but not the other way around.

questions.question: Write down all subsets of {a, b, c} and verify the number is 2³.
questions.answer: Subsets of {a, b, c}: ∅, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a, b}, {a, c}, {b, c}, {a, b, c}. Total: 8 = 2³. Confirms |P(A)| = 2^|A|.

questions.question: What is the difference between a subset and a proper subset?
questions.answer: A is a SUBSET of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is in B. A is a PROPER SUBSET of B (A ⊂ B) if A ⊆ B AND A ≠ B. Every set is a subset of itself (A ⊆ A) but not a proper subset of itself.

questions.question: Apply inclusion-exclusion: in a class of 60 students, 30 take Maths, 25 take Physics, and 15 take both. How many take Maths or Physics?
questions.answer: n(M ∪ P) = n(M) + n(P) − n(M ∩ P) = 30 + 25 − 15 = 40 students. So 40 take at least one of the two subjects; 60 − 40 = 20 take neither.

questions.question: Prove that A − B = A ∩ B' for any two sets A and B.
questions.answer: x ∈ A − B ⟺ (x ∈ A) and (x ∉ B) ⟺ (x ∈ A) and (x ∈ B') ⟺ x ∈ A ∩ B'. Since the two sets have the same elements, A − B = A ∩ B'. (This identity is often used to convert set differences into intersections during proofs.)

questions.question: Verify De Morgan's first law for U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}.
questions.answer: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3}; (A ∪ B)' = U − {1, 2, 3} = {4, 5}. A' = {3, 4, 5}; B' = {1, 4, 5}; A' ∩ B' = {4, 5}. Both sides equal {4, 5} — De Morgan's first law verified.

questions.question: Verify De Morgan's second law for U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}.
questions.answer: A ∩ B = {3}; (A ∩ B)' = U − {3} = {1, 2, 4, 5}. A' = {4, 5}; B' = {1, 2, 5}; A' ∪ B' = {1, 2, 4, 5}. Both sides equal {1, 2, 4, 5} — De Morgan's second law verified.

questions.question: List the power set of {0, 1}.
Using a Venn diagram, illustrate (A ∩ B)' and identify which region it shades.
questions.answer: Draw U as a rectangle, A and B as two overlapping circles. (A ∩ B)' is the COMPLEMENT of the overlap region — i.e. everything in U EXCEPT the lens-shaped intersection. So shade the entire rectangle, but leave the overlap of A and B unshaded. Equivalently (by De Morgan): shade A' ∪ B', which is everything outside A union everything outside B.

questions.question: Prove the distributive law A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
questions.answer: x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ A AND x ∈ (B ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ A AND (x ∈ B OR x ∈ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A AND x ∈ B) OR (x ∈ A AND x ∈ C) [distributive law of AND over OR in logic] ⟺ (x ∈ A ∩ B) OR (x ∈ A ∩ C) ⟺ x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). Hence the two sets have the same elements and are equal.

questions.question: Show with an example that set difference is NOT commutative.
questions.answer: Take A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}. A − B = {1} (elements of A not in B). B − A = {4} (elements of B not in A). {1} ≠ {4}, so A − B ≠ B − A. Hence set difference is not commutative.

questions.question: Find the symmetric difference of A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}.
Give one example of a finite set and one of an infinite set, with justification.
questions.answer: Finite: A = {x : x is a prime number less than 10} = {2, 3, 5, 7}. It has exactly 4 elements. Infinite: B = {x : x ∈ N, x is even} = {2, 4, 6, 8, ...}. It has no largest element, so it cannot be listed in a finite way.

questions.question: Why is the power set of A always strictly larger than A itself (i.e. |P(A)| > |A| for any finite A)?
questions.answer: For any finite set A with n elements, |A| = n and |P(A)| = 2^n. For all n ≥ 0, 2^n > n (proved by induction: 2⁰ = 1 > 0; if 2^k > k then 2^(k+1) = 2·2^k > 2k ≥ k+1 for k ≥ 1). So the power set is always strictly larger. (This generalises to infinite sets too — Cantor's theorem — but the finite case is enough here.)

questions.question: In a survey, 70 people read newspaper A, 60 read newspaper B and 30 read both. How many read at least one? How many read only A? How many read neither (if total surveyed is 120)?
questions.answer: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 70 + 60 − 30 = 100 read at least one. Only A = n(A) − n(A ∩ B) = 70 − 30 = 40. Neither = 120 − 100 = 20.

questions.question: If A = {1, {2, 3}, 4}, list all the SUBSETS of A. How many are there?
questions.answer: A has 3 elements: 1, {2, 3}, and 4. (Note: {2, 3} counts as ONE element of A.) So |A| = 3 and |P(A)| = 2³ = 8. Subsets: ∅, {1}, {{2,3}}, {4}, {1, {2,3}}, {1, 4}, {{2,3}, 4}, {1, {2,3}, 4}. Note the double braces around {2,3} when it appears as a subset's element.

questions.question: State the inclusion-exclusion principle for two sets. In a class of 80 students, 50 like Maths, 40 like Science, and 20 like both. Find: (a) the number who like Maths or Science, (b) the number who like exactly one of the two, (c) the number who like neither.
questions.answer:
Inclusion-exclusion (two-set version): n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). This counts elements in either A or B but subtracts the double-count of those in both.

(a) n(M ∪ S) = 50 + 40 − 20 = 70. So 70 students like at least one of the two.

(b) Exactly one = n(M ∪ S) − n(M ∩ S) = 70 − 20 = 50. (Or equivalently: only-M + only-S = (50 − 20) + (40 − 20) = 30 + 20 = 50.)

(c) Neither = 80 − n(M ∪ S) = 80 − 70 = 10.

Summary: 30 like only Maths, 20 like only Science, 20 like both, 10 like neither. Total: 30+20+20+10 = 80 ✓.

questions.question: State and prove De Morgan's laws for two sets A and B with respect to the universal set U.
questions.answer:
STATEMENT. For any sets A, B (subsets of universal set U): (i) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'  and  (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

PROOF OF (i): x ∈ (A ∪ B)' ⟺ x ∈ U and x ∉ (A ∪ B) ⟺ x ∈ U and NOT(x ∈ A or x ∈ B) ⟺ x ∈ U and (x ∉ A) and (x ∉ B)  [De Morgan's law in logic] ⟺ (x ∈ A') and (x ∈ B') ⟺ x ∈ A' ∩ B'.

Since the two sets have exactly the same elements, (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'.

PROOF OF (ii): Apply (i) with A and B replaced by A' and B' respectively: (A' ∪ B')' = A'' ∩ B'' = A ∩ B. Take complement: A' ∪ B' = (A ∩ B)'. Equivalently: (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

VERIFICATION (example): U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4, 5}. (A ∪ B)' = {1,2,3,4,5}' = {6}. A' ∩ B' = {4,5,6} ∩ {1,2,6} = {6} ✓. (A ∩ B)' = {3}' = {1,2,4,5,6}. A' ∪ B' = {4,5,6} ∪ {1,2,6} = {1,2,4,5,6} ✓.

questions.question: In a group of 200 people, 80 like coffee, 70 like tea, 60 like milk, 20 like both coffee and tea, 30 like both tea and milk, 25 like both coffee and milk, and 10 like all three. How many like at least one of the three drinks? How many like exactly one?
questions.answer:
Use the three-set inclusion-exclusion principle:
n(C ∪ T ∪ M) = n(C) + n(T) + n(M) − n(C ∩ T) − n(T ∩ M) − n(C ∩ M) + n(C ∩ T ∩ M).

Substitute: = 80 + 70 + 60 − 20 − 30 − 25 + 10 = 210 − 75 + 10 = 145.

At least one: 145 people.

Exactly one: only-C + only-T + only-M.
only-C = n(C) − n(C∩T) − n(C∩M) + n(C∩T∩M) = 80 − 20 − 25 + 10 = 45.
only-T = 70 − 20 − 30 + 10 = 30.
only-M = 60 − 30 − 25 + 10 = 15.
Exactly one = 45 + 30 + 15 = 90.

Verification: like none = 200 − 145 = 55.

questions.question: Prove the associative and distributive laws for sets: (a) A ∪ (B ∪ C) = (A ∪ B) ∪ C, and (b) A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
questions.answer:
(a) ASSOCIATIVITY OF UNION. x ∈ A ∪ (B ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ A or (x ∈ B or x ∈ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) or x ∈ C [associativity of 'or' in logic] ⟺ x ∈ (A ∪ B) or x ∈ C ⟺ x ∈ (A ∪ B) ∪ C. Hence the two sets are equal.

(b) DISTRIBUTIVE LAW (union over intersection). x ∈ A ∪ (B ∩ C) ⟺ x ∈ A or (x ∈ B and x ∈ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) and (x ∈ A or x ∈ C) [distributive law of 'or' over 'and'] ⟺ (x ∈ A ∪ B) and (x ∈ A ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C). Equality of the two sets follows.

Note: there is a symmetric distributive law A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C), proved by the same logic with 'and' over 'or'.

questions.question: Define a power set. List the power set of (a) ∅, (b) {a}, (c) {a, b}, (d) {a, b, c}. Observe the pattern of |P(A)|.
questions.answer:
Definition: the power set P(A) of a set A is the set of all subsets of A (including ∅ and A itself).

(a) P(∅) = {∅}. |P(∅)| = 1 = 2⁰.

(b) P({a}) = {∅, {a}}. |P({a})| = 2 = 2¹.

(c) P({a, b}) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}. |P({a, b})| = 4 = 2².

(d) P({a, b, c}) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a, b}, {a, c}, {b, c}, {a, b, c}}. |P({a, b, c})| = 8 = 2³.

Pattern: |P(A)| = 2^|A|. Each element of A can independently be in or out of a given subset, giving 2^n possibilities.

questions.question: Using De Morgan's laws, simplify ((A ∪ B)' ∩ C')'.
questions.answer:
((A ∪ B)' ∩ C')' = ((A ∪ B)')' ∪ (C')'  [De Morgan's second law: (X ∩ Y)' = X' ∪ Y']
           = (A ∪ B) ∪ C  [using (X')' = X applied twice]
           = A ∪ B ∪ C.

So the original expression simplifies to A ∪ B ∪ C. Quick verification: pick A = {1}, B = {2}, C = {3}, U = {1,2,3,4}: A ∪ B = {1,2}; (A ∪ B)' = {3,4}; C' = {1,2,4}; (A ∪ B)' ∩ C' = {3,4} ∩ {1,2,4} = {4}; complement is {1,2,3} = A ∪ B ∪ C ✓.

questions.question: Using Venn diagrams (describe in words), verify the distributive law A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
questions.answer:
Draw the universal set U as a rectangle and three overlapping circles A, B, C inside it (a standard three-set Venn diagram with 8 regions including the outside-everything region).

LHS — A ∩ (B ∪ C): first shade B ∪ C (the union of circles B and C). Then take the part of A that lies inside this shaded region. Result: the portion of A that overlaps with B or with C (or both).

RHS — (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C): A ∩ B is the lens where A and B overlap (regardless of C). A ∩ C is the lens where A and C overlap. The union is everything in A that overlaps either B or C.

Both descriptions pick out exactly the same regions of the Venn diagram (the portion of A that intersects B ∪ C), so the two sets are equal. Algebraic and pictorial views agree.

Quick numerical check: A={1,2,3}, B={2,4}, C={3,5}. B ∪ C = {2,3,4,5}; A ∩ (B ∪ C) = {2,3}. A ∩ B = {2}; A ∩ C = {3}; (A∩B) ∪ (A∩C) = {2,3} ✓.

questions.question: In a survey of 1000 households, 750 own a television, 600 own a mobile phone, 200 own neither. How many own both? How many own only a TV?
questions.answer:
Total owning at least one = 1000 − 200 = 800.

By inclusion-exclusion: n(TV ∪ Mobile) = n(TV) + n(Mobile) − n(TV ∩ Mobile) ⇒ 800 = 750 + 600 − n(TV ∩ Mobile) ⇒ n(TV ∩ Mobile) = 1350 − 800 = 550 own both.

Only TV = n(TV) − n(TV ∩ Mobile) = 750 − 550 = 200 own only a TV.
Only Mobile = 600 − 550 = 50 own only a mobile.
Neither = 200.
Total: 200 + 550 + 50 + 200 = 1000 ✓.

questions.question: Using De Morgan's laws, prove the identity A − (B ∪ C) = (A − B) ∩ (A − C).
questions.answer:
Recall A − X = A ∩ X'. Start from the LHS:
  A − (B ∪ C) = A ∩ (B ∪ C)'  [definition of difference]
            = A ∩ (B' ∩ C')   [De Morgan's first law]
            = (A ∩ A) ∩ (B' ∩ C')  [since A ∩ A = A — idempotent]
            = (A ∩ B') ∩ (A ∩ C')   [associativity + commutativity]
            = (A − B) ∩ (A − C)     [definition of difference, twice]

So LHS = RHS, the identity is proven. (Companion identity: A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C), proved similarly with the second De Morgan law.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A school surveys its 150 senior students about extracurricular activities. 80 play cricket, 70 play football, and 30 play both.

(i) How many play at least one of cricket or football?
(ii) How many play only cricket?
(iii) How many play only football?
(iv) How many play neither cricket nor football?

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

At a juice bar 300 customers ordered drinks. 200 had orange juice, 180 had apple juice, and 80 had both.

(i) How many ordered juice (at least one of the two)?
(ii) How many ordered exactly one juice?
(iii) How many ordered neither?
(iv) If 50 customers also ordered pineapple juice (independent of O and A), what's the maximum possible number who ordered all three?
questions.answer:
(i) n(O ∪ A) = 200 + 180 − 80 = 300. Every customer had at least one of the two.
(ii) Exactly one = n(O ∪ A) − n(O ∩ A) = 300 − 80 = 220.
(iii) Neither = 300 − 300 = 0. Every customer ordered some juice.
(iv) Maximum n(O ∩ A ∩ P) ≤ min(n(O), n(A), n(P)) = min(200, 180, 50) = 50. So at most 50 customers ordered all three.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

In a class of 60 students, 30 study Hindi, 35 study English, 25 study Sanskrit. 15 study both Hindi and English, 12 study both English and Sanskrit, 10 study both Hindi and Sanskrit, and 5 study all three.

(i) How many study at least one language?
(ii) How many study only Hindi?
(iii) How many study only English?
(iv) How many study none of the three?

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A company runs three departments: Tech (T), Sales (S), Marketing (M). The CEO needs to assign committees of any size (including the empty committee).

(i) If T has 4 members, how many possible committees can be formed from T alone?
(ii) If S has 5 members, how many committees include EVERY member of S?
(iii) How many committees from M (which has 3 members) have at least one member?
(iv) What does this tell you about the relationship between subsets and committees?
questions.answer:
(i) Subsets of a 4-element set = 2⁴ = 16 committees.
(ii) Only one — the whole set S. There's only one subset that contains every element of S, namely S itself.
(iii) 2³ − 1 = 7 (excluding the empty committee from the 2³ = 8 subsets).
(iv) Forming a committee from a set IS exactly the same as picking a subset. So the number of possible committees = the number of subsets = 2^n. The empty committee corresponds to the empty subset. This is why combinatorial 'how many ways to choose' questions reduce to subset-counting.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A student claims: 'For any sets A and B, the complement of (A ∪ B) equals A' ∪ B'.' Another student says: 'No, by De Morgan's law, (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'.'

(i) Which student is correct? Justify.
(ii) Construct a small counter-example to show the first student's claim is wrong.
(iii) State both De Morgan's laws.
(iv) Explain the intuition behind De Morgan's laws using a Venn diagram description.
questions.answer:
(i) The second student is correct. (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' by De Morgan's first law.
(ii) Counter-example: U = {1, 2, 3, 4}, A = {1}, B = {2}. A ∪ B = {1, 2}; (A ∪ B)' = {3, 4}. A' = {2, 3, 4}; B' = {1, 3, 4}; A' ∪ B' = {1, 2, 3, 4} = U. Clearly (A ∪ B)' = {3,4} ≠ U = A' ∪ B'. The first student's claim is false.
(iii) De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
(iv) Venn picture: (A ∪ B)' is everything OUTSIDE both circles A and B. Equivalently this is the region OUTSIDE A AND OUTSIDE B, which is A' ∩ B'. Similarly (A ∩ B)' is everything outside the overlap region, i.e. outside A OR outside B = A' ∪ B'. The laws turn 'union' into 'intersection' (and vice versa) when you take a complement.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Consider the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

(i) How many subsets does A have?
(ii) How many subsets contain the element 3?
(iii) How many subsets do NOT contain the element 3?
(iv) What relationship exists between answers (ii) and (iii)?
questions.answer:
(i) 2⁵ = 32 subsets.
(ii) Fix 3 in the subset; freely choose each of the other 4 elements: 2⁴ = 16.
(iii) Forbid 3 from the subset; freely choose the other 4: 2⁴ = 16.
(iv) They are equal! 16 + 16 = 32 = total subsets. For any specific element, exactly half the subsets contain it and exactly half don't. This is true for any single element of any non-empty finite set.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A set A has 5 elements and a set B has 3 elements.

(i) What is the maximum possible value of |A ∪ B|?
(ii) What is the minimum possible value of |A ∪ B|?
(iii) What is the maximum possible value of |A ∩ B|?
(iv) Under what condition is |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|?
questions.answer:
(i) Max |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| = 5 + 3 = 8 — achieved when A and B are disjoint.
(ii) Min |A ∪ B| = max(|A|, |B|) = 5 — achieved when B ⊆ A.
(iii) Max |A ∩ B| = min(|A|, |B|) = 3 — achieved when B ⊆ A.
(iv) |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| holds iff |A ∩ B| = 0, i.e. A and B are disjoint (no common elements). This is the cleanest case of inclusion-exclusion: nothing to subtract.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A student writes down the following four sets: A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {a, b, c}, C = {3, 2, 1}, D = {1, 2, 3, 4}.

(i) Which pair is EQUAL?
(ii) Which pair is EQUIVALENT but not equal?
(iii) Is any pair DISJOINT?
(iv) Which pair satisfies A ⊂ D?
questions.answer:
(i) A and C are equal (same elements: 1, 2, 3 — order doesn't matter).
(ii) A and B are equivalent (both have 3 elements) but not equal (different elements).
(iii) Yes — A and B are disjoint (no common element). Also C and B are disjoint.
(iv) A is a proper subset of D (every element of A is in D, but A ≠ D). C ⊂ D for the same reason.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

The Venn diagram of two sets A and B is divided into four regions by the boundary of U: outside both A and B; only in A; only in B; in both A and B.

(i) Which region represents A ∩ B?
(ii) Which region represents A − B?
(iii) Which region represents (A ∪ B)'?
(iv) Which two regions together represent the symmetric difference A △ B?
questions.answer:
(i) A ∩ B = the central lens-shaped overlap of the two circles.
(ii) A − B = the part of circle A that is OUTSIDE circle B (i.e. the crescent of A excluding the overlap).
(iii) (A ∪ B)' = the region OUTSIDE both circles, inside the rectangle U.
(iv) A △ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A) = the two crescents — the part of A not in B, plus the part of B not in A. (Everything in exactly one of the two sets.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A library has 1000 books. 500 are fiction, 400 are non-fiction, 100 are reference (R), and 50 books fit into more than one category in this scheme. Categories are not exclusive.

(i) What is the maximum possible n(F ∪ N ∪ R)?
(ii) Some books are in NO category (unsorted). If 950 books are sorted into at least one of F, N, R, how many are unsorted?
(iii) Suppose 30 books are in F ∩ N. What is the minimum value of n(F ∪ N)?
(iv) Could n(F ∩ R) = 150? Why or why not?
questions.answer:
(i) Max n(F ∪ N ∪ R) = min(n(F) + n(N) + n(R), 1000) = min(500 + 400 + 100, 1000) = min(1000, 1000) = 1000. (Achievable only if there's no overlap at all, i.e. all are in exactly one category and totals match.)
(ii) Unsorted = 1000 − 950 = 50.
(iii) n(F ∪ N) = n(F) + n(N) − n(F ∩ N) = 500 + 400 − 30 = 870.
(iv) No. n(F ∩ R) ≤ min(n(F), n(R)) = min(500, 100) = 100. So 150 is impossible — F ∩ R cannot exceed the smaller of |F| and |R|.
